entry.title: IDA Documentary Awards 2026 Nominations: ‘You Can See Everything,’ ‘Concrete Land,’ and More Earn Nods
entry.summary: See the nominations for the 42nd annual IDA Documentary Awards, which will take place December 4, 2026, at The Ebell of Los Angeles.
entry.content:
On Tuesday, November 17, the International Documentary Association (IDA) announced the nominees for its 42nd annual IDA Documentary Awards, including everything from the highly publicized blockbuster “You Can See Everything” to under-the-radar Best Documentary Feature contenders like “Concrete Land.”

“I couldn’t be more excited to celebrate these meaningful and creative documentaries. It’s a challenging time for documentary makers, but also a really inspiring moment for IDA and for the field,” IDA Board President Ina Fichman said in a statement. “This year we see nominees whose deeply personal stories share narratives of resistance and exile, and we see artful, innovative filmmaking that is capturing new and robust audiences. I hope many will join us on December 4 as we honor our incredible community.”

Related Stories
A24’s TV Division Is Quietly Having as Strong a Year as Its Film Team
‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Throws Netflix’s Oscar Campaign a Curveball

The 2026 IDA Documentary Awards will also present the following special honors: the Career Achievement Award for the late Chilean filmmaker Patricio Guzmán; the Truth to Power Award for Amy Goodman and Juan González of Democracy Now!; the Emerging Filmmaker Award for Maia Lekow and Christopher King; and the Amicus Award for Cannes Docs, the documentary program of the Marché du Film led by Pierre-Alexis Chevit.

This year, IDA received a record 650 entries in all categories from 95 countries, an increase over last year both in the total number of entries and the countries represented. 32 countries are represented among the final lineup of nominees.

IDA members from around the world will vote for the winners in the Best Feature Documentary and Best Short Documentary categories from November 17 to November 29, 2026. All other category winners are selected by juries representing the international documentary community.

The Awards will take place December 4, 2026, at The Ebell of Los Angeles, hosted for the second year in a row by documentary field leader Tabitha Jackson.

Nominees in each category are listed in alphabetical order by film title.

entry.title: A24’s TV Division Is Quietly Having as Strong a Year as Its Film Team
entry.summary: With shows like "Crystal Lake," "Euphoria," and "Margo's Got Money Troubles," A24 has ramped up its output and landed shows on every major streamer.
entry.content:
Maybe it’s just because we can’t get enough headlines and discussion about “Backrooms” and “You Can See Everything,” but despite the banner year A24 has had at the box office, its TV division has quietly had nearly as strong of a year.

The indie label has produced more shows in 2026 than in any year in its history, including sleeper commercial and critical hits across the board, and even managed to land shows on virtually every streamer in town.

Led by Sam French, the U.S. head of TV at A24, the studio this year has cranked out the third season of “Euphoria” on HBO Max, the second season of “Beef” and the third season of “Survival of the Thickest” both on Netflix, “Margo’s Got Money Troubles” on Apple TV, the “Friday the 13th” prequel series “Crystal Lake” on Peacock, and most recently the British sitcom “It Gets Worse” on Paramount+ led by the UK Heads Piers Wenger and Rose Garnett. Its unscripted division, led by Johnny Hausfater, has also ramped up aggressively, with shows like “Neighbors,” “Born to Bowl,” and “Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow” all on HBO Max.

Related Stories
Sean Connery Wasn’t the First James Bond: Meet Barry Nelson in the ‘Casino Royale’ You’ve Never Seen
‘The Other Bennet Sister’ Christmas Special Trailer: Can Mary Bennet Still Be Herself and ‘the Perfect Wife’?

Not unlike its film slate, its series have been a blend of auteur-driven prestige and genre shows with a twist. The David E. Kelley series “Margo’s Got Money Troubles” is a tongue-in-cheek, real-world satire on motherhood and the modern economy about a young single mom played by Elle Fanning who needs to turn to OnlyFans for extra cash. On the other side of the coin, “Crystal Lake” follows masked killer Jason Voorhees’ mom and stands out from other modern horror TV shows by, as our critic wrote, not trying to secretly be a family drama or a slapstick comedy or some other genre or metaphor, but it just amplifies the grisly kills in the best way it can.

The recurring theme between these shows isn’t genre but the stamp of quality that A24 lends.

While something like “Beef” saw a steep drop in viewership of a reported 60 percent between its first and second seasons, “Euphoria” in its return was up 17 percent in its finale ratings compared to Season 2. “Crystal Lake” was also a big hit on Peacock, its top show on the streamer last month, logging 1.3 billion minutes watched over its first 11 days, making it the fourth-highest scripted original series ever on Peacock. A24 now has roughly 30 to 40 shows in various stages of development, pre-production, or active production, with its executive team expanding from about 15 from just 3 people in its early days.

It’s been able to ramp up firstly because of its partnership with numerous TV buyers across the major streamers, but also because of working with largely first-time creators and showrunners. While “Crystal Lake” is a notable exception, A24 generally is operating on its TV side the same way it does with its film, leading with the artist and the project they want to pursue rather than the IP.

That has produced some very personal and idiosyncratic projects over the years like “Ramy” and “The Curse,” the latter of which was the kernel of getting Nathan Fielder to working with A24 again on “You Can See Everything.”

The breadth of content A24 has amassed on its TV side and continually making shows that have the same barrier-pushing flavor and stamp of quality that has become known with A24’s brand is what will help make it as essential a part of the company’s overall business and valuation as its film and distribution business. But we’re seeing even its TV division branching out and embracing IP and tentpoles in the same way its film side has.

Coming up for A24 are a Claire Danes and Ewan McGregor drama “The Spot” on Hulu and “The Apology” with Gwyneth Paltrow on Netflix, which already got a two-season order and was an example of a show that grew out of Paltrow being convinced to try TV after already working with A24 on the film side for “Marty Supreme.” The studio is also is working with Ben Stiller on a New York Knicks documentary series for HBO and a competition cooking show based on the video game “Overcooked” for Netflix. A24 could’ve made a Knicks series with anyone, but teaming with a superfan like Stiller was another example of putting the creator above the concept.

Yet, both a strength and weakness of its TV model is that it does not have a distribution mechanism the way it does on the film side. It’s not bogged down with an unprofitable streamer, a dwindling linear cable channel, or a broadcast network, but that makes it reliant on the many partners it has built up across the industry.

Warner Bros. merging with Paramount arguably reduces the buyers in the market, even if there are still two streamers at Skydance. Netflix just had a massive shakeup of its leadership team that could easily have a different attitude toward A24’s series. And the overall industry trends around the end of Peak TV mean it’s always a volatile business for independents in the TV space.

But no one saw “Backrooms” or “You Can See Everything” coming either, and A24 has as good a chance as any to have lightning strike twice with the next “Euphoria” or “Beef.”

entry.title: ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Throws Netflix’s Oscar Campaign a Curveball
entry.summary: Netflix has to campaign the follow-up to Oscar winner 'Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,' but is that a distraction from its more viable contenders?
entry.content:
From a purely awards-hunting perspective, there’s a great argument to be made that Netflix could have pushed back its late November release “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” until next year. Historically, the perception of the embattled studio is that its had issues being distracted by too big an awards slate to pin down its Best Picture frontrunner. Remember in 2023 when it seemed like the streamer did not realize until the Oscar shortlists (in mid-December!) that “All Quiet on the Western Front” was its best bet at Best Picture? The Edward Berger film went on to win four Oscars, including Best International Feature.

Related Stories
How ‘Paper Tiger’ Evolved When Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway Couldn’t Reprise Their ‘Armageddon Time’ Roles
Sean Connery Wasn’t the First James Bond: Meet Barry Nelson in the ‘Casino Royale’ You’ve Never Seen

This year, Netflix is running their best awards campaign yet with “La Bola Negra,” which the studio acquired out of Cannes, where its helmers, Los Javis, won the jury prize for Best Director. Come the fall festivals, it became the first Netflix film to win the People’s Choice Award at TIFF. Since then, it has fronted Netflix’s experiment in expanding the theatrical distribution of its awards slate, doing admirable business in key markets. The consensus among prognosticators is that the film is not only a lock to receive a Best Picture nomination, but is also sure to win the Oscar for Best International Feature on behalf of Spain.

If Netflix wanted to secure a second Best Picture nomination, with “Cliff Booth” out of the picture, the team could put all its energy into Lee Chang-dong’s “Possible Love.” Not only is the near-three hour film, which won the Grand Jury Prize at Venice, another Best International Feature contender (on behalf of South Korea), but it is one of this season’s most critically lauded films. If enough critics’ groups get behind it in the coming weeks, a la “The Secret Agent” last year, then a second Best Picture nomination for Netflix at the 2027 Oscars becomes highly plausible.

Somewhere along the way, “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” became something of a puzzle for Netflix. The streamer had no choice but to follow through with putting it out around Thanksgiving, because it was already set to replace the IMAX screens that had initially been secured for Greta Gerwig’s “Narnia” film. So how does a company not run an awards campaign for the sequel to a recent Best Picture nominee, directed by a three-time Oscar nominee, written by a two-time Oscar winner, and starring Brad Pitt in the role he just won a Best Supporting Actor Oscar for?

What reads as a home run on paper is more of a double or triple in execution. “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is made by people who know what they are doing, and that expands past director David Fincher, screenwriter Quentin Tarantino, and star Pitt.

Cinematographer Erik Messerschmidt, editor Kirk Baxter, production designer Donald Graham Burt, set decorator Jan Pascale, and composers Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross have all won at least one Academy Award. Costume designer Trish Summerville was nominated for an Oscar for her work on “Mank.” Even if there is a low bar for getting the Academy excited about a late-’70s period piece set in Hollywood, “Cliff Booth” easily clears it.

But we are in a spectacle-heavy year, with “The Odyssey” and “Project Hail Mary” in the awards conversation, and “Dune: Part Three” and “Werwulf” on the horizon. Even “Digger” is a formidable contender in the craft races. So if the feeling is that “Cliff Booth” is more of a hangout movie than a cinematic event, then the focus of its awards campaign should be on categories that are more willing to embrace that, like Best Production Design or Best Costume Design. (Not so much Best Sound, which “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” did actually receive nominations for.)

In terms of the acting performances, again, Pitt is great as Cliff Booth, but there is no rush to nominate him for a performance he already won for. And there are plenty of other Best Actor contenders, like Matt Damon and John Malkovich (who have never won) and John Turturro and Andrew Scott (who have never even been nominated for an Oscar before).

The top performance of the film is with Cliff’s love interest, played by Emmy winner Elizabeth Debicki, who actually does have a shot at her first Oscar nomination, given the love for her performance in “Wicker” as well, and the lack of current consensus in the Best Supporting Actress race.

Everyone else in the film, from Scott Caan to Yahya Abdul-Mateen II to Carla Gugino, is very additive to the project but does not necessarily cross the threshold into Oscar-contender territory. In that way, it is similar to Tony Gilroy’s “Behemoth!,” another awards hopeful from this season.

Ultimately, “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is entertaining enough to garner support from certain branches of the Academy, but falls too late in the year, in too few theaters, to truly become the last-minute surprise blockbuster that would get as many as 10 Oscar nominations, something its predecessor “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” did handily.

entry.title: How ‘Paper Tiger’ Evolved When Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway Couldn’t Reprise Their ‘Armageddon Time’ Roles
entry.summary: James Gray interview: How ‘Paper Tiger’ evolved when Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway couldn't reprise their ‘Armageddon Time’ roles.
entry.content:
Editor’s Note: The following story contains spoilers for “Paper Tiger.”

James Gray never hid that Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway were playing fictional versions of his real-life parents in his 2022 drama “Armageddon Time,” based on the writer/director’s experience as a sixth grader growing up in Queens in the 1980s.

“Jeremy is doing my father to such a degree that it is disturbing.  He sounds exactly like him, looks exactly like him; it’s bizarre. Annie, too, is uncanny about [playing my mother],” said Gray while a guest on this week’s episode of IndieWire’s Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast. “So I had had such a great time with them shooting ‘Armageddon Time,’ I said, ‘Well, why don’t we do this again?’”

Related Stories
Sean Connery Wasn’t the First James Bond: Meet Barry Nelson in the ‘Casino Royale’ You’ve Never Seen
‘Madden’ Review: David O. Russell Fumbles Again with an Unfunny and Purposeless Football Biopic

Gray knew his next film (what would become “Paper Tiger”) would be set in 1986 and once again focus on a Jewish family of four, with two sons, in Queens. In the project’s early stages, Hathaway and Strong were up for reprising their roles, but it soon became clear Gray would have to wait 18 months — after both “The Odyssey” (Hathaway) and “The Social Reckoning” (Strong) finished filming — to start production.

“You can’t wait a year and a half,” said Gray. “And then I started thinking, ‘Well, maybe this is a blessing in disguise.’ That the [film] could start to take on a new style, and so then I started to pursue it in a different way. So in the beginning, in its origin stages, it was [a sequel of sorts], but like any movie, it’s like a wild horse that’s going to get away from you.”

While Scarlett Johansson and Miles Teller’s characters in “Paper Tiger” are inspired by Gray’s parents, they are not as deeply grounded as Hathaway and Strong were in “Armageddon Time” as facsimiles of Gray’s parents in how they talked, looked, dressed, and behaved. Through this lens, Gray began to see the film as less of a straight memoir, freeing him to embrace elements of the crime genre in his storytelling.

Explained Gray, “What I tried to do was to make a film more in — for lack of a better way of really explaining — a bit more Hitchcockian in certain places. Almost — again, ‘pulpy’ is not quite the right word — a little bit more, how do I put this — more of an engagement directly with a tense idea of narrative, that it would be a driving, tense story.”

What also changed is the sympathetic lens through which Gray now saw his father. In “Paper Tiger,” Irwin (Teller) puts his family in danger when he unwittingly gets entangled (pursuing environmental consulting work for businesses along the polluted Gowanus Canal) with the Russian mob. While Irwin is guilty of pride and naivety, it is (especially compared to Gray’s previous films) a positive portrayal of a hard-working and earnest father pursuing the American dream.

In this sense, the shift from Strong to Teller was fortuitous. Strong had painted an unforgiving portrait of a miserable, strict father — tortured by generational trauma and unbending with his sons striving for upward mobility — whereas Gray saw something in Teller he could lean into for a different portrayal of his father.

“Miles has a kind of — I can’t believe I’m going to say this, he might even resist this— a softness to him, which would probably offend him, but I think that’s a great thing,” said Gray. “He doesn’t have a softness in his persona. He doesn’t have it in physical terms. It’s actually a tenderness inside. You have to embrace [that] beauty in him and hope it works for the film.”

When it came to recasting Hathaway, Gray was more practical, saying he needed three characteristics: another bankable star, who was also Jewish, and a real New Yorker. He believed the way the city seeps itself into a person’s bones is not something that even the best actors can learn to portray. Those three unnotiables made Scarlett Johansson the clear number one choice.

“I had met [Scarlett] years before on a project that never wound up happening, and quite liked her. She’s a total New Yorker through and through. Then when I found out that Annie [Hathaway] was going off to do Chris [Nolan’s] movie [‘The Odyssey’] for a thousand years, she was the first choice because you’re talking about one of the biggest stars in the world, and she’s also a Jewish woman from New York,  checks the boxes,” said Gray. “When I sent [the script] to her, I sent her a note, ‘There’s probably no chance in hell you’re going to do this, but I love you, can you read this?’ And then she texted me back very, very quickly and was like, ‘Let’s go.’”

While Hathaway’s portrayal of Gray’s mother was more open and loving than Strong’s version of his father — and therefore didn’t require as sharp a contrast in how the role was recast — Gray believed Johansson’s approach better fit the needs of “Paper Tiger.”

“It’s a more operatic idea of character than Annie’s was in ‘Armageddon Time,’” said Gray. “It’s much more a kind of high emotion. And of course, because the situation is much more tragic, and she embraced it completely.”

“Paper Tiger” opened last weekend in New York and Los Angeles, and expands on November 20.

To hear James Gray‘s full interview, subscribe to the Filmmaker Toolkit podcast on Apple, Spotify, or your favorite podcast platform. You can also watch the full interview on YouTube.

entry.title: Sean Connery Wasn’t the First James Bond: Meet Barry Nelson in the ‘Casino Royale’ You’ve Never Seen
entry.summary: 'The Shining' actor Barry Nelson introduced Ian Fleming's James Bond in a 1954 television adaptation of 'Casino Royale' before Sean Connery.
entry.content:
Ever since George Lazenby first replaced Sean Connery as James Bond in 1969’s “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service,” fans have argued over who makes the best 007 — and those arguments are likely to resume once Robert Pattinson takes the screen as the latest Bond in director Denis Villeneuve’s new iteration. Although Craig has his partisans, Connery tends to be the consensus choice for the best Bond, though I’ve argued here for the merits of 1970s and ’80s Roger Moore. All the Bonds have their virtues, but Connery benefited from being there first — for anyone who discovered the series in its initial heyday, Connery simply is James Bond.

Related Stories
‘The Other Bennet Sister’ Christmas Special Trailer: Can Mary Bennet Still Be Herself and ‘the Perfect Wife’?
‘Madden’ Review: David O. Russell Fumbles Again with an Unfunny and Purposeless Football Biopic

Yet Connery actually wasn’t the first actor to play Bond. That honor goes to journeyman MGM contract player Barry Nelson, who played Bond in a “Casino Royale” adaptation eight years before Connery made the character famous in “Dr. No.” Connery may have been the first 007 to grace the big screen, but Nelson established Bond on the small screen in an episode of the CBS anthology series “Climax!” opposite Peter Lorre in the Le Chiffre role that would later be inhabited by Orson Welles (in the goofy 1967 “Casino Royale”) and Mads Mikkelsen (in the 2006 adaptation that introduced Craig to the series).

The 1954 “Casino Royale” is a fascinating artifact that includes elements that would go on to characterize future James Bond movies, while also going in a few other very different directions. The key difference is in the scale, stripped down by necessity for television production. The hour-long “Climax!” episode is all interiors, taking place entirely in the hotel and casino of the title. It’s more a James Bond play than a movie, with Bond and Le Chiffre facing off in a series of verbal — and ultimately physical — jousts in confined spaces, and it’s surprisingly effective.

It’s also a very strange beginning for a franchise that would come to be known for its globetrotting locales and elaborate action set pieces. Not that this “Casino Royale” was officially part of the James Bond franchise as we know it. In fact, although there have been three adaptations of Ian Fleming’s first James Bond novel, only the third incarnation with Daniel Craig was from EON Productions, the company that controlled the character from “Dr. No” through the Craig era before selling the rights to Amazon.

The 1954 “Casino Royale” came about when producer Gregory Ratoff optioned the rights to Fleming’s novel in May of that year. The novel wasn’t yet a hit, and Fleming was sorely in need of cash, which led him to make one of the worst deals in movie-rights history when he sold the book outright to Ratoff for $6,000 after the TV episode aired. This left “Casino Royale” out of the deal when EON secured the screen rights to James Bond as a character, so Bond producers Albert Broccoli and Harry Saltzman could only sit back and grit their teeth when Ratoff turned “Casino Royale” into a comedy in 1967 and cast Peter Sellers, David Niven, Woody Allen and others as rotating Bonds.

EON ultimately made a deal to bring “Casino Royale” under their umbrella and used the novel to reboot the franchise with Craig, but in 1954 it served as the source for a much more modest affair. The biggest similarities between the 1954 “Climax!” episode and the Daniel Craig movie come in the time spent on extended gambling sequences, and the centering of a brutal torture scene. Given censorship restrictions of the time, Nelson’s torture in a bathtub is considerably less graphic than the mallet to the testicles inflicted on Craig, but it’s rough enough stuff for a 1950s TV production.

Certain aspects of Nelson’s characterization, like Bond’s mix of sexual swagger and icy indifference, would later be adopted by most future 007s, to varying degrees. The biggest difference between Nelson and future Bonds is a simple one: He’s American. Although Broccoli and Saltzman flirted with the idea of an American Bond throughout the series’ history (going so far as to cast James Brolin in “Octopussy” before Moore decided to return at the last minute), to date they’ve never actually pulled the trigger on casting outside the UK.

Nelson is probably best known to modern audiences as the affable hotel manager Stuart Ullman in Stanley Kubrick’s “The Shining,” but in the 1950s he was a sturdy character actor and occasional leading man who bounced around television after an initial sojourn as a studio contract player. As a young man, he appeared in several important MGM films, including “Shadow of the Thin Man,” “Bataan,” and “A Guy Named Joe” (the source material for Steven Spielberg’s “Always”). Later on, he popped up in “Airport” and had a successful Broadway career. He was nominated for a Tony acting opposite Liza Minnelli in Martin Scorsese’s 1977 production “The Act.”

In 1954, though, he was in the middle of a prolific and productive era as a TV stalwart, both as a series regular (on “The Hunter” and “My Favorite Husband”) and a frequent guest star. He doesn’t exhibit a ton of range as American “Combined Intelligence” agent “Jimmy” Bond, but that too is in keeping with the overall conception of the character, at least until Craig tried to bring a little more emotional depth to the role.

In Americanizing Bond, the “Climax!” edition of “Casino Royale” ends up making a number of related changes that are small but make the film feel just a bit off for fans of the EON productions. American Felix Leiter (later played by Jeffrey Wright) becomes Brit Clarence Leiter, for example. Although there’s none of the Bond gadgetry that would become famous later, there are hints of what’s to come in the form of props like a villain’s cane that hides a gun, and the opening credits for the “Climax!” series itself feature a gun barrel pointed at the viewer that predicts the iconic graphics of later Bond title sequences.

The 1954 “Casino Royale” is noteworthy for another reason: its composer, Jerry Goldsmith, who would ultimately score hundreds of major films, including “Planet of the Apes,” “Chinatown,” “Basic Instinct,” and most of Joe Dante’s work. Yet in some ways what’s fascinating about “Casino Royale” is how unremarkable it is — it’s a decent, solid piece of entertainment from an era when proliferating anthology shows provided similar programs every week.

If Fleming had his way, it would have only been the start for 007 on television; he wrote several outlines for episodes of a James Bond series before CBS canceled the project. Luckily, he repurposed most of what he wrote as short stories for his 1960 book “For Your Eyes Only,” and television’s loss was cinema’s gain. By 1962, James Bond belonged to the movies — and to Sean Connery.

entry.title: ‘The Other Bennet Sister’ Christmas Special Trailer: Can Mary Bennet Still Be Herself and ‘the Perfect Wife’?
entry.summary: The smash hit BritBox series will return this winter with three very specials, and one heck of a surprise for fans of Caroline Bingley.
entry.content:
Any news about the upcoming “The Other Bennet Sister” Christmas special — three episodes released in time for Christmas, but not set at Christmas — is worthy of celebration, but the first trailer for the upcoming BritBox treat also packs one heck of a wallop for fans of breakout character Caroline Bingley. Brace yourselves!

Following the first 10 episodes of the smash hit series, based on Janice Hadlow’s novel of the same name, these three new episodes pick up after the very happy ending of the first season finale. But while the marriage of Mary Bennet (Ella Bruccoleri) and Tom Hayward (Dónal Finn) was an unabashedly joyous occasion, the special dares ask: well, now what? Or, more appropriately, how does someone like Mary retain her unique qualities and serve as a “perfect wife”?

Related Stories
Movie Theaters Are Back, but the Rest of Hollywood Seems to Be Crumbling
’14th’ Trailer: Ava DuVernay Unpacks the Necessity of Another Essential Constitutional Amendment

That’s a tall enough order, and that’s before (gasp) the return of Caroline Bingley (Tanya Reynolds) and Mr. Ryder (Laurie Davidson), who return back to London from their jaunt to Italy with lots of big reveals. We won’t spoil anything that the trailer doesn’t, but the three episodes look to already have plenty of drama long before the Ryders (yes, you read that correctly) come back into the fold with a baby in tow. We’re scandalized and delighted.

Also returning for the special are Ruth Jones as Mrs. Bennet, Varada Sethu as Ann Baxter, Poppy Gilbert as Lizzie Darcy, Maddie Close as Jane Bingley, Grace Hogg-Robinson as Lydia Wickham, Molly Wright as Kitty Buncock, and Anna Fenton-Garvey as Charlotte Collins. Nerys Amber Stocks also joins the cast as Mary’s housemaid Lucy. Screenwriter Sarah Quintrell also returns, writing all three additional episodes of the special. Asim Abbasi has also returned to direct.

BritBox also announced today that its podcast series “On the Box” will launch “On the Box with The Other Bennet Sister” video companion episodes. Following each installment of the special, executive producer Jane Tranter and stars Bruccoleri, Finn, Reynolds, and Davidson join hosts Edith Bowman and Michelle Collins to “unpack the episode, share behind-the-scenes stories, and discuss key moments from the series.” The official companion podcast episodes will be available to watch and listen on BritBox and wherever podcasts are available as soon as each episode premieres.

Episodes of “The Other Bennet Sister” special will debut weekly on BritBox. BritBox Premier subscribers, who enjoy early access to select programming and additional features, will be able to binge all three episodes of the special early. Check out the special’s first trailer below.

entry.title: ‘Madden’ Review: David O. Russell Fumbles Again with an Unfunny and Purposeless Football Biopic
entry.summary: Would it surprise you to learn that Nicolas Cage in a fat suit doesn’t a compelling film make?
entry.content:
“Madden” is technically a David O. Russell film, but all involved seem to want to downplay that fact. Amazon MGM Studios, in their infinite wisdom, has decided to emphasize star Nicolas Cage’s performance as the larger-than-life NFL coach and sports broadcaster in its scant promotional material. While the trailer includes an obligatory “From the director of ‘Silver Linings Playbook’ and ‘American Hustle’” title card, the poster features Cage and Christian Bale, who plays Oakland Raiders coach Al Davis, flashing their Super Bowl rings, and no mention of Russell. Even the PR flack at the sparsely-attended press screening introduced the film by saying, “Please enjoy Nicolas Cage’s ‘Madden’!”

Related Stories
Skydance Sets Film Leadership Team: Don Granger and Kira Goldberg to Head Paramount Motion Picture Group, Jesse Ehrman Promoted to WB Pictures Chief
Movie Theaters Are Back, but the Rest of Hollywood Seems to Be Crumbling

To be fair, this isn’t the worst promotional strategy. Russell may be a problematic figure, but it wasn’t so long ago when starring in one of his films almost guaranteed an actor awards attention. During a brief five-year period in the 2010s, his work garnered Oscar wins for Christian Bale and Jennifer Lawrence, and nominations for Amy Adams, Bradley Cooper, and Robert De Niro. Putting aside the uneven quality of his work, Russell certainly afforded actors the opportunity to “make choices” in lavish studio productions, which often amounted to adopting broad accents and wearing flashy costumes, and receive acclaim for their efforts. It’s probably why people keep working with him in spite of the numerous incidents of on-set mistreatment (on top of a sexual assault allegation) that have continued to this day.

Russell may shifted to streaming but his commitment to allowing actors to go big or go home remains sacrosanct. In “Madden,” Cage wore 30 pounds of prosthetics on top of the 25 pounds he gained for the role. He certainly resembles the man, at least if you ignore Cage’s actual face. Ditto Bale, who adopts Davis’s Noo-Yawk accent and bold fashion sense. But it’s all in service of a film so milquetoast that it will make you beg for the sheer personality exhibited in “Amsterdam,” which at least had the decency to have a narrative and occasionally spark tension and generally be about something.

Here’s what happens in Russell’s eleventh feature: head coach John Madden leads the Oakland Raiders to finally beat their longstanding rivals Pittsburgh Steelers in the 1976 AFC Championship, after which they win the Super Bowl. Following his diagnosis of a bleeding ulcer in his stomach, Madden permanently retires from his coaching career to be with his family. Realizing he’s a stranger in his own home after spending too much time away, he quickly transitions into sports broadcasting where he becomes a television mainstay. To secure his legacy and pass on his legendary playbook, he eventually lends his likeness to EA Sports for the “Madden” video game franchise, which becomes one of the most profitable on the market. He then lives happily ever after.

If that sounds like a film with little-to-no conflict, you would be correct. Part of the problem is that Madden, while being an American institution and a legendary NFL coach, isn’t really suited to be the subject of a biopic, largely because the details of his life are fairly free of drama or intrigue. He’s the kind of figure who should be the lead of a Saturday-morning cartoon where he helps kids solve mysteries using the power of his football mind. Rather than impose a zany plot onto his life or make up outlandish shit for entertainment purposes, which he’s known to do, Russell dutifully relates the major events in his life.

The bare-bones emotional foundation of “Madden” takes the form of the two loves in the eponymous character’s life. The first is with his wife Virginia (Kathryn Hahn), who longs for John to recommit to fatherhood and their marriage, at least until it becomes clear that he needs football to be a functioning human being. Hahn’s established joie de vivre ensures Viriginia is slightly more interesting than an archetypal long-suffering wife character, but, alas, her general lack of chemistry with Cage dampens their tender scenes together, and their intermittent marital troubles are too fleeting and half-hearted to make any dramatic purchase.

The second, and arguably most pivotal, is with Davis, whose slightly-problematic bromance with Madden serves as the film’s primary source of drama. Russell’s film briefly flirts with an interesting thread by portraying Davis as a devil on Madden’s shoulder, someone who seemingly wants him to continue coaching forever, his health and family life be damned. He constantly tries to pressure Madden into returning to the league long after he retires in the vein of an old buddy who wants you to stay out for “just one more beer.” Despite his size, Madden frequently shrinks in Davis’s presence, who knows just what to say to get him to do what he wants.

But while Russell gestures towards connecting Davis’s “maverick” professional style, which made him uniquely qualified for the world of sports ownership but nevertheless created controversy within the league, and his friendship with Madden, he ultimately chickens out from characterizing him as a truly malign influence. (“Madden” just isn’t set up to be a film with a villain or an antagonist of any kind.) Instead, Russell depicts John and Virginia Madden and Al and Carol (Sienna Miller) Davis as tightknit couple friends, admittedly a type of relationship that rarely receives the big-screen treatment, whose ups and downs are manageable because, well, they really just love each other.

It’s worth noting that “Madden” is technically a comedy. It certainly presents as one, featuring well-proven settings for laughter in sports comedies like the sidelines, the locker room, and the announcing booth. Intermittent jokes pop up in these spaces, though I’m genuinely hard-pressed to remember anything specific because much of it suffocates under Cage’s affectionately-caricatured performance. Russell trusts that the sight of the actor in a full-body fat suit is enough for audiences. Granted, Cage seems to palpably enjoy embodying Madden’s flamboyant energy and imposing figure, even if his inconsistent voice acting, complete with slurred speech and vowel-swallowing, occasionally threatens to tip into outright cruelty. (“Madden” features the real article speaking at the film’s end and it’s downright absurd how much Cage exaggerates his diction.)

If there’s one semi-sophisticated bit in the film, it’s that Madden’s one-track mind sees the world entirely through football strategy. He literally can’t write “XOXO” to his future wife in their yearbook without turning it into a play design. But Russell doesn’t really develop the idea any further and instead defaults to broad humor that tends to blend together and subsequently die on the vine. These often materialize as sight gags, like Bale’s increasingly ridiculous haircuts, or John Mulaney, who plays Electronic Arts founder Trip Hawkins, costumed to resemble Steve Jobs. Sometimes it amounts to Shane Gillis delivering Shane Gillis-style lines, sometimes with a perm or donning a wizard’s outfit, or former running back Marshawn Lynch dressed like a nerd.

On paper, Russell is actually a neat fit for a film like “Madden.” He made his bones directing abrasive ensemble screwball comedies. He’s directed period biopics, including one that’s also a sports drama, and one of his most acclaimed films involves football fandom. Sadly, “Madden” features few Russellisms beyond tacky ’70s and ’80s fashion and some mild domestic discord. He’s replaced his typically messy, chaotic atmosphere for an overly genial one.

Anyone who has some familiarity with screen passes or end-arounds likely learned it downwind from Madden, who used whiteboards to make complicated play schemes accessible to the viewing public. His impact extends well into the realm of pop culture, like the Miller Lite commercial where he breaks through the wall, the custom-manufactured bus in which he drove around the country due to his well-documented fear of flying, and his famous turducken. “Madden” covers all of that material without offering any insight other than the security of the man’s legacy. The Russell who made “I Heart Huckabees” has long faded away, but it’s still a shame that he’s been reduced to directing one of the oddest and blandest examples of brand management in recent memory.

Grade: D+

Amazon MGM Studios will release “Madden” in select theaters and on Prime Video on Wednesday, November 18.

entry.title: Skydance Sets Film Leadership Team: Don Granger and Kira Goldberg to Head Paramount Motion Picture Group, Jesse Ehrman Promoted to WB Pictures Chief
entry.summary: Skydance has tapped Don Granger and Kira Goldberg as motion picture group presidents at Paramount, while setting WB's leadership.
entry.content:
Skydance has set its film leadership team.

Don Granger, a veteran Skydance executive, and Kira Goldberg, a leader of Netflix’s film team, have been tapped as presidents of Paramount‘s Motion Picture Group.

As part of the moves, Jesse Ehrman has been promoted to president of Warner Bros. Pictures, while Mikey Ireland will remain as president of production. Their task will be to stabilize Warner Bros.‘ film output while rejuvenating or extending franchises like “The Lord of the Rings” and “The Conjuring.” Skydance executives have been horrified by the extent of the losses racked up by Pam Abdy and Michael De Luca, with sources estimating them in the hundreds of millions of dollars. David Ellison, who orchestrated Warner Bros.’ merger with Paramount, was more diplomatic on a recent earnings call, though he said the WB film division has “underperformed this year.”

Related Stories
‘Madden’ Review: David O. Russell Fumbles Again with an Unfunny and Purposeless Football Biopic
Movie Theaters Are Back, but the Rest of Hollywood Seems to Be Crumbling

As part of this restructuring, Jeff Goldstein, who oversaw Warner Bros. distribution for many years, will retire, and Bill Damaschke will exit Warner Bros. Pictures Animation, which he led. Skydance said that in the interim, Jennifer Dodge and Traci Balthazor will oversee all animation across both Paramount and Warner Bros. Pictures. Richard Brener, a survivor of several mergers, will remain as president and chief content officer of New Line, where he guided hits like “Weapons.”

Others remaining include: Lia Buman, EVP, head of global acquisitions and Republic Pictures; J.D. Lifshitz and Raphael Margules, heads of the genre division, Paramount Primal; and Christian Parkes, head of the indie label Clockwork; and Charlie Tabesh, SVP and general manager of Turner Classic Movies.

Last week, Skydance announced that James Gunn and Peter Safran, who had led DC Studios, were leaving the company. Jeremy Latcham, a former Marvel executive, replaced them. It wasn’t the only overhaul at the top. Last month, as Skydance took full control of Warner Bros., Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy were ousted. De Luca and Abdy were beloved by the creative community, but they spent liberally and accumulated too many flops, including “Digger” and “The Bride!”

Both Granger and Goldberg will report to Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein, the co-chairs of Skydance’s Motion Picture Group. Across Paramount and Warner Bros., the mandate will be to get more films into production. To get the merger over the finish line, Skydance founder David Ellison agreed to make more than 30 films annually, far exceeding the output of any traditional studio.

In a memo to staff, Goldberg and Greenstein praised Granger as “a great partner as we’ve repositioned the studio, bringing in key talent relationships and nearly doubling output.” They noted that at Netflix, Goldberg “oversaw a slate that included ‘Don’t Look Up,’ starring Leonardo DiCaprio and Jennifer Lawrence, and the upcoming ‘Bad Day,’ with Cameron Diaz, and ‘The Take’ starring Denzel Washington and Robert Pattinson. Goldberg was also an executive at Fox, working on films such as “The Greatest Showman” and “Bohemian Rhapsody.”

“Together, Don and Kira will work hand in hand going forward,” Goldberg and Greenstein wrote, adding, “We have both an incredible legacy to build upon and an enormous opportunity ahead of us: to champion the world’s best filmmakers, invest in ambitious storytelling and deliver an unparalleled slate of films that captivate audiences everywhere.”

Ehrman is a WB veteran who has worked on hits such as “A Minecraft Movie” and “Sinners.” Ireland joined Warner Bros. after years at Paramount. He left the studio after it was sold to Skydance in 2025.

“This team brings deep knowledge of our businesses, strong creative instincts and longstanding relationships across the industry,” Goldberg and Greenstein wrote. “We have tremendous confidence in these leaders and are grateful for their partnership.”

entry.title: Movie Theaters Are Back, but the Rest of Hollywood Seems to Be Crumbling
entry.summary: Movie theaters staged a dramatic rebound in 2026, but the struggles of Netflix, Skydance and other entertainment companies show Hollywood is flailing.
entry.content:
Movie theater owners have been through hell.

The pandemic forced many of them to shut their doors for months. When they could finally turn their marquees back on, Omicron and other variants made audiences skittish about returning to cinemas. Then the writers’ and actors’ strikes upended production, leaving them with fewer movies to screen. A promised moviegoing revival kept getting delayed or disrupted, often by circumstances outside of the exhibition industry’s control.

At long last, things are finally changing. Domestic ticket sales are up 20 percent year over year, and with potential blockbusters like “Dune: Part Three,” “Avengers: Doomsday,” and “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” on the horizon, analysts expect revenues to easily eclipse $10 billion for the first time since COVID. Grosses in North America currently sit at $8.76 billion through November 15, fueled by franchise fare such as “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and “Toy Story 5,” but also by unconventional hits ranging from “Project Hail Mary” and “The Odyssey” to “Obsession” and “You Can See Everything.”

Related Stories
Desire, Death, and a Breakthrough Year for Queer Cinema
‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Review: They Shoot Franchises, Don’t They?

Audiences are showing up for superhero movies and three-hour documentaries about a convicted felon. And media companies, which treated the theatrical business as the sick man of the entertainment industry, are finally seeing the value in cinemas, with the likes of Amazon MGM Studios and Skydance committing to making more movies for the big screen than most major studios did over the last decade. Better yet, younger viewers are driving the comeback, with studies showing that Gen Z members are the most frequent moviegoers.

That’s the good news. Elsewhere, Hollywood seems to be crumbling. Netflix, which has done more to reshape the entertainment industry this century than arguably any other company, is teetering, having jettisoned both chief content officer Bela Bajaria and film chief Dan Lin in a brutal purge. Ted Sarandos, who is clearly feeling the heat after the company’s stock has fallen 35.6 percent year-to-date, has brought in Peter Rice, a well-regarded former Fox and Disney exec whose calm demeanor and unthreatening good looks are out of c-suite central casting, to steady the ship.

But Netflix shares have yet to recover, even after the company laid off more than 1,000 employees. Part of the problem is that Netflix, which has introduced everything from ad-based tiers to live sports to boost subscribers, still hasn’t figured out a strategy to combat its biggest competitor: YouTube. Last summer, the online video giant overtook Netflix in average daily viewing worldwide, and its popularity is only growing. How will Netflix keep building its user base? That’s the question vexing Sarandos and Netflix’s investors, and there’s no easy answer.

It’s not like things are going much smoother across the entertainment industry. As the decade dawned, most major studios zeroed in on Netflix as their chief rival, opting to build in-house streaming services to challenge it for cultural supremacy. Thus, we were gifted with Disney+, HBO Max, Paramount+, and Peacock, which battled for a finite pool of viewers while spending wildly. The streaming boom quickly went bust. The issue was that no matter how many new subscribers they attracted, streaming profits paled in comparison to what they made from linear television, where they raked in money through a mix of advertising and retransmission fees. Everyone recognized that streaming was the future and that customers were cutting the cord, but offering them a cheaper, streaming alternative threatened to accelerate that transition. That’s a problem because these companies need the cash flow from cable to fund all their other operations.

As Hollywood has stumbled around trying to develop a better business model, the solution that many companies have landed on is to get bigger, fast. Thus, Fox sold to Disney, MGM was auctioned off to Amazon, and David Ellison’s Skydance bought Paramount and then quickly merged it with Warner Bros. Others, such as Comcast, spun off assets to make themselves more digestible. Has it worked? That’s the $80 billion question at Skydance, where executives have pledged to make 30 movies a year and turn a combined Paramount+ and HBOMax into a true Netflix challenger. Yet Ellison must pull this off while paying down a massive amount of debt.

So far, their early moves haven’t inspired much confidence. Executives like CBS News chief Bari Weiss have embraced the Silicon Valley ethos of “move fast and break things,” but what they’ve built instead, such as a simulacrum of “60 Minutes,” doesn’t seem better than what they’ve replaced. And if, as a recent Variety story about Skydance’s post-merger strategy suggests, part of their cost savings involves making sure executives don’t send out for “sandwiches and green juices” from Erewhon, they’re in for a world of pain. They can have Jimmy John’s cater lunch, and it won’t make a dent in their debt.

Skydance has already laid off most of Warners’ leadership and offered buyouts to the rank-and-file. Another wave of layoffs is expected at the company any day now. And across town, those types of cuts are the default move, with everyone from Disney and NBCUniversal to Amazon and Sony slashing hundreds of jobs. Are some of these layoffs in anticipation of what a leaner, AI-assisted future might bring? Probably. But with many of these companies’ share prices flatlining or falling, they aren’t being enacted out of foresight or a position of strength.

“I can’t remember a time when things have felt so scary,” an entertainment executive confessed to me recently.

And they’re right. It’s always popular to say the movie business is dying or the television industry is collapsing, and those doomsayers have been proven wrong time and time again. People want to be entertained. It’s just that making money entertaining them has never been harder for Hollywood.

entry.title: Desire, Death, and a Breakthrough Year for Queer Cinema
entry.summary: LGBTQ+ films like 'La Bola Negra,' 'Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma,' and 'Elsinore' explored desire and death in fresh ways.
entry.content:
A willingness to die for sex is a familiar bargain for queer people. Born in the twentieth century at the wrong place and time? Beware of Nazis, AIDS, and other mortal dangers. Hollywood has at times depicted these threats in ways that emphasize the humanity of LGBTQ+ people, as when Tom Hanks played a lawyer dying of AIDS in “Philadelphia,” during the height of the epidemic in 1993. The industry also has a history of finding ever more creative ways to kill off and scapegoat queer characters, a trope that as recently as 10 years ago seemed to be running amok.

But a more twisted and nervy dance between desire and death has unfolded in this year’s spate of particularly macabre queer films. After years of what felt like permanent advances in rights and representation, LGBTQ+ people have been stung by backlash, including attacks on gender-affirming care, legal threats to marriage equality, and cuts to suicide prevention. Amid a reduced perception of safety, anxieties about the possibilities and consequences of nonnormative desire are spilling out onscreen like so much fake blood. Even so, their formulation is evidence of social and creative progress.

Related Stories
‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Review: They Shoot Franchises, Don’t They?
‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ First Reactions: Quentin Tarantino and David Fincher Deliver a ‘Pure Riot’ of a Hangout Movie

This alarm has played out, perhaps most obviously, in horror films. In Adrian Chiarella’s “Leviticus” and Jane Schoenbrun’s “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma,” same-sex attraction engenders extreme and potentially deadly terror, be it from detractors or the people it consumes. Both films explore not the evils of queerness — an argument that belongs to the tradition of queer-coded villains — but the horrors of having one’s desires villainized.

The year’s queer history films also subvert conventional narratives around sexuality and deadly fates. In Andrew Scott’s awards-season vehicle “Elsinore,” Ian Charleson’s dying wish to play Hamlet is one many actors would share; the film doesn’t focus on how or why he has AIDS, but what he wants to do before it kills him. The Spanish epic “La Bola Negra” depicts forbidden romance, but desire isn’t what dooms its multiple generations of queer men. The fact that they’re swept up in the currents of history, just like everyone else, is part of the film’s revolutionary power.

The era for combatting the notion that being gay is a no good, very bad thing in a straightforward way finally seems to have passed. Usually such sermons were preaching to the choir anyway. Gone is the teary earnestness of a conversion therapy drama like “Boy Erased,” from 2018, in which much of the trauma wrought on Lucas Hedges’ character derives from the church but is carried out by earthly messengers. In “Leviticus,” when a healer tries to pray the gay away from a pair of lovesick adolescents, he conjures supernatural and murderous doppelgangers.

After rituals of deliverance are performed over the convulsing bodies of a pair of schoolmates (played by Joe Bird and Stacy Clausen), each one is haunted by an illusion of the other that tries to kill them. The concept of “Leviticus,” named for the Old Testament book that forbids man to lie with man, partly functions as a wry play on the idea that you never get over your first crush. It also takes the fear that so many queer people know well — that what you desire most will be your downfall — to literal and horrifying extremes. Imagining the bigotry of organized religion as a senselessly violent supernatural force is a radical reversal. The boys aren’t the problem; the boogeymen that torment them spring from the so-called good book.

Schoenbrun’s meta queer fantasia “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” likewise performs a canonical revision. The nonbinary killer in the campy franchise within the film were themselves killed and sunk to the bottom of a lake by their comically gender-panicked peers. A victim seeking revenge, the TV-headed slasher is called Little Death, a nod to a French term for orgasm, la petite mort. Hannah Einbinder’s millennial filmmaker is on a quest to reboot the franchise, but more significantly, to achieve her own “little death.” In order to grow more comfortable with sex, and give into her own desires, her fear of intimacy — one that, again, many queer people know well — needs to be killed.

The movie ultimately intertwines fear of death with the fear of intimacy in a way that demonstrates the stakes — how you can feel so afraid of getting close to someone you could just die. But what must be slaughtered in this case is fear itself — so that same-sex desire, which has so often been pathologized and villainized, can flourish. (The trail of straight people extravagantly dispatched along the way, like so many gays before them, is one of the film’s many deranged and delightful flourishes.)

There is a potent realignment evident in the year’s period films as well, which center the desires and fates of queer characters on their own terms, rather than taking their oppression or disease as subjects unto themselves. “Elsinore” leans a bit heavily on obvious sentiment while leaving much of the thematic richness of “Hamlet” on the table. But Charleson’s determination to play the part before he dies is what drives the film, while the indignities of succumbing to AIDS are mostly a secondary plot.

Contrast that with recent period dramas on TV, like “It’s a Sin” (2021) about young people facing the AIDS crisis in London, or “Fellow Travelers” (2023) about the Lavender Scare in the U.S., and focusing on Charleson’s dream itself rather than the injustice of what threatens it marks a distinct shift.

The broad sweep of the canvas in “La Bola Negra” heralds another major turn of the page. The play of the same name by Federico García Lorca that partly inspires the movie, and appears in one of its several timelines, is about a young man denied access to an elite social club because he’s presumed to be gay. But homophobia isn’t the primary struggle (or a harbinger of death) for the film’s other gay characters. It certainly doesn’t help two doe-eyed young men (played by Miguel Bernardeau and Guitarricadelafuente) brought together and kept apart by the Spanish Civil War. But the forbiddenness of their infatuation is just one current swirling around them, the most pressing of which is, well, the Spanish Civil War.

Weaving the fates of queer characters into the broader scope of history, and suggesting a lineage of ancestry and shared desire, as “La Bola Negra” so marvelously does, feels like a kind of imaginative reparations. And it marks a bolder, more robust tactic in humanizing queer lives; the film traces generational ties and uncovers untold histories, rather than contending with acute crises like religious doctrine or deadly disease.

There is a stranger and more expansive creative palette evidenced in these films, one that suggests the unnerving climate for queer people in the real world is only furthering the reaches of the imagination. In carrying forward the legacy of queer cinema, it seems the gays presumed buried by the trope are finally rising up.

entry.title: ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Review: They Shoot Franchises, Don’t They?
entry.summary: Read our review of 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,' the sixth installment in the 'Hunger Games' franchise.
entry.content:
A grimmer, gloomier “Hunger Games” is on the horizon with “Sunrise on the Reaping,” adapted from Suzanne Collins’ prequel novel about the origin story of the hardened alcoholic Haymitch Abernathy. Here, the teenage version of Woody Harrelson’s character in the original films is played by Australian actor Joseph Zada, the blond, ringletted Adonis who also starred as the moody Cal Trask in the recent “East of Eden” series.

Franchise fans might be riveted by Francis Lawrence’s latest installment — points for consistency, as he’s directed all the films dating back to 2013’s “Catching Fire” — but those audiences not already invested in the dystopian material and tales of tributes will find themselves left out in the cold by an overlong (it’s 158 minutes, so get comfortable), visually soupy, and narratively morose reprisal. But no matter, as this new slice of bankable I.P. is likely to rake in a hysterical amount of money, and perhaps launch Zada’s career as a face of new Hollywood stardom.

Related Stories
‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ First Reactions: Quentin Tarantino and David Fincher Deliver a ‘Pure Riot’ of a Hangout Movie
‘Hershey’ Review: An Unbelievably Flavorless Biopic About America’s Most Famous Chocolatier

The film is set during the 50th Hunger Games, otherwise known as the Second Quarter Quell. Only 16 years old, Haymitch is thrust into games that are rigged from the start — and whose broadcasting is ultimately edited and deepfaked to look like pro-Capitol propaganda. (The film nudges a little bit toward the ethics of state surveillance and how footage can be manipulated or even fabricated for political ends.) His pastoral, if impoverished, life in District 12 is small but happy, with girlfriend Lenore (Whitney Peak) and a mother and younger brother (Kara Tointon and Smylie Bradwell) with whom he shares close affinity, plus a best friend we’ll eventually find out will become the father of Katniss Everdeen (Lawrence) in the later films.

After a reaping (refresher: that’s when tributes are selected ceremonial-style, here as by a grotesquely pulled-tight-in-the-face Glenn Close as Drusilla Sickle) turns bloody, long-shot Haymitch ends up being selected at only 16. Violence follows him everywhere, as during the subsequent Tribute Parade, tragedy strikes Haymitch’s childhood friend (Molly McCann) during a horse-drawn Tribute chariot ride. Sequences meant to be thrilling often lack connective tissue to the rest of the material, or are devised in such a maelstrom of CGI (as goopy and cacophonous as a Marvel battle) that it’s difficult to feel engaged. It’s also unhelpful that most of the supporting cast is so wildly over the top, especially Capitol residents played by Close and a smarmy and mannered Kieran Culkin. Jesse Plemons as a Hunger Games camera operator brings a shade of moral dimension to the proceedings, but as with his “Digger” role, the actor feels woefully underused. Ralph Fiennes as Capitol president Snow, meanwhile, is given but scraps of material to work with.

The by-the-book script by Billy Ray and Michael Lesslie appears to stick faithfully to Collins’ 2025 novel, with plenty of potential for visual appeal that goes largely unrealized. The Hunger Games arena Haymitch is thrust into is rife with hidden dangers: poisonous streams, a deadly force field, and other trippy flora and fauna that vibe like a dark mirror version of “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory,” but again, “Sunrise on the Reaping” trips up on the CGI fakery.

The movie’s stacked young cast of tributes and mentors (those victors of previous Hunger Games tournaments) includes Mckenna Grace as a District 12 tribute who’s not to be trusted, the endearingly wily Ben Wang (recently excellent in the SXSW film “Brian”), plus a gravely underused Maya Hawke as the winner of the 49th Hunger Games, Kelvin Harrison Jr. as victor of the 34th, and the great Lili Taylor as a legacy tribute played previously by Lynn Cohen (aka Magda on “Sex and the City”) in the second film. These characters mostly exist to introduce themselves to Haymitch, be established as good or evil or helpful or unhelpful, and then be shuffled out of the scene. Elle Fanning is rather amusing, however, as the Capitol stylist Effie Trinket, styled and nearly drowned out by extremely outré fashions. Glenn Close also (with a visage channeling Katherine Helmond as Ida Lowry in “Brazil”) could’ve been used to better effect.

The specter of death looming over the film should not be confused for much in the way of actual depth, and while Zada’s performance is charming enough, his character lacks the gravitational charisma or arc that, say, Jennifer Lawrence brought to the original films. He feels like a cog or a function to get this prequel to line up with the prior films — and isn’t that what he is? Which makes the movie, and ergo probably the book, feel a little bit like a cold cash grab rather than a necessary deepening of the series’ lore. When Haymitch comes home from Second Quarter Quell and descends into depression and alcoholism, that’s when the movie gets most interesting. Not a great sign when your film’s tepid coda is also its best moment.

And equally worrying is a series of cameos tacked onto the film’s end that smack of depressing fan service. These movies seem to be mostly critic-proof and hugely appealing to their core audience, but “Sunrise on the Reaping” is a dreary slog, another death-march “They Shoot Horses, Don’t They?” riff with a pretty Gen Z cast, and one that mistakes new layers of darkness (and trauma!) for the sort of profundity that its filmmakers hope will burnish a creatively withering property.

Grade: C-

“The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” opens in theaters on Friday, November 20.

entry.title: ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ First Reactions: Quentin Tarantino and David Fincher Deliver a ‘Pure Riot’ of a Hangout Movie
entry.summary: 'The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth' has premiered. Read the first reactions.
entry.content:
Few films on the 2026 calendar felt like bigger question marks than “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.” The prospect of Brad Pitt reprising his Oscar-winning role from “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” in a Netflix pseudo-sequel written by Quentin Tarantino but directed by David Fincher was not on many people’s bingo cards when the project was first announced. The fact that the news originally broke on April Fool’s Day even led some people to wonder if the whole thing was an elaborate joke.

But the crowd who made their way to the TCL Chinese Theater on Monday, November 16 can attest that “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is very much real. The film was introduced by Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos, who joked that he instantly greenlit the film after receiving an 11-word text from Fincher that simply read “Written by Quentin Tarantino. Directed by David Fincher. Starring Brad Pitt.” As Sarandos tells it, he simply responded “Yes.”

Related Stories
‘Hershey’ Review: An Unbelievably Flavorless Biopic About America’s Most Famous Chocolatier
‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Returning to Theaters with a New Rosario Dawson Cameo — and Box Office Records and Oscar Noms in Mind

When the lights went down, the crowd was treated to a rollicking hangout movie filled with elaborate recreations of ’70s Los Angeles, classic rock and soul needle drops, and a meandering plot that blends crime and comedy into one elaborate excuse for Pitt’s Cliff Booth to wander around the city exuding charisma. It wasn’t long before the social media reactions began to flow in, many of which were quite positive.

The online buzz following the premiere praised Pitt’s willingness to do seemingly anything (a few scenes seem destined to go very viral), his romantic chemistry with Elizabeth Debicki, and the film’s unapologetic commitment to capturing both the Los Angeles of yesteryear that Booth inhabited and the style of movie that he loved to watch. And of course, there are plenty “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” Easter Eggs to go around.

“The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is set to debut for a two-week exclusive engagement in IMAX Theaters globally on November 25, 2026, before debuting on Netflix on Wednesday, December 23. Keep reading for a roundup of social media reactions following the film’s premiere.
